COAL TRANSPORT CON 2024

By: Nicky Troll | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Coal theft like you’ve never seen it before. A new MO that's the ball game of stealing coal!

Summary:
We know the drill - opportunistic criminals target transport company drivers to steal loads and loads of coal for a fee. BUT now, the expose the latest trend.

The real coal mafia is hard work as coal theft has evolved into a sophisticated criminal network – the modus operandi have morphed and we will be exposing a brand new one.


Further information:
COAL THEFT 3.0 - THE EVOLUTION OF COAL THEFT

UNDERSTANDING THE PROCESS
1. Transporters will be contracted to move tons of coal from a mine (POINT A) to a processing plant or power station or railway station for export (POINT B).
2. Collection slips are issued when the trucks are loaded at POINT A.
3. At POINT B – delivery notes are issued when the loads are dropped off.

THE THEFT - not all the loads make it from POINT A to POINT B. Some loads are stolen out right while others switched with a lesser grade of coal.
a. Drivers are approached by a middleman to drop the load off at another location along the route between A & B for a fee of R2500 – R12000.
b. Delivery notes are jippo-ed and the receiving company at POINT B is none the wiser of the loss.

COAL THEFT 3.0 THE EVOLUTION OF COAL THEFT
This time round criminal syndicates have streamlined their thieving operations.

THE NEW MO
1. A legitimate transporter has a contract from a mine to move coal from Point A to Point B. In this case from Belfast to Richardsbay for export.
2. This transporter is approached by a smaller transport company with 15 trucks asking for work – the transporter does due diligence, and appoints the smaller company as a sub-contractor.
3. The sub-contractor collects 50 loads from the mine, and gives the transporter that contracted them all the paper work stating the load were delivered – the stamped delivery notes, photos of the sealed loads – everything that’s required.

BUT ALL IS NOT AS IT SEEMS
The mine contacts the transporter – 50 loads were never received – the paper work was forged. No loads collected by the sub-contractor was EVER delivered. Those 50 loads were stolen.

THIS SUB-CONTRACTOR GOT THE JOB WITH THE SOLE PURPOSE OF STEALING!!!

HOW BIG IS THE PROBLEM?
This is not an isolated problem – coal theft plagues the industry across South Africa. The black market for coal is thriving because there is a huge demand for coal locally and for export. So if you can get a cheap load that you can sell at premium prices – dodgy dealers are willing to look the other way.

LOSSES
The stolen loads would have been paid for the company meant to receive the cargo because the paperwork in terms of the jippo-ed delivery notes will check out. But the dodgy dealers buying the stolen loads will then re-sell the cargo back into the market – essentially one loads would be paid for TWICE!

Because there are insiders involved, the paperwork checks out – but it is only when stock takes are done by the receiving companies that the losses are noted. For example, a company would have paid for 100 000 tones, but only received 80 000.


INTERVIEWS
INDUSTRY EXPERT – SCHALK DU PREEZ
DU PREEZ heads up the coal theft investigations for a group of mines - he will explain the black market and how these syndicates have evolved their modus operandi’s incorporating tech and elaborate schemes to steal coal – it’s no longer the odd dodgy driver – it’s the coal mafia at work.

TRANSPORTER – ANTON EICKER

WE GO IN SEARCH OF SHIYEKA ENTERPRISES

** ADDITIONAL SHOOT
INTERVIEW WITH TRACKER
Confirming the tracking logs were forged.

INTERVIEW OPS MANAGER OF THE TRANSPORTER
They’ve been able to find at three more transporters were the same MO was used – not necessarily the same broker, but the same method – getting a contract with the sole purpose of stealing, using fake number plates – some of which correspond with Eicker Transport.

** ADDITONAL LINKS
** ADDITIONAL B-ROLL

PART THREE: TRANSPORT COAL SALES CON - 10 min

VO: In the heart of coal country, legitimate transport businesses are under siege from criminal networks running rampant with new devious tactics.

REPEAT FROM LATER - KEEP END CLIP IN PLACE… TEASERING….
GOVAN- Here comes another one, no - something is happening here // let’s go see…
GUY: I DON’T DO CAMERAS

A BEAT… 2 seconds

SCHALK: Behind this is greed, it’s money, big money.

VO: Schalk du Preez is a Mining Security consultant.

SCHALK: Traders are creating the market because if there's no market, then there's no draw, no carrot for the thieves to steal the coal.

VO: But killing the stolen coal market is easier said than done.

With the demand for coal - skyrocketing globally and locally - hitting a record high in 2023 - criminal syndicates are quick to take advantage.

LINK: Coal theft has evolved, drivers stealing load by load and selling it off. Really just bottom feeders. The most sophisticated criminal networks have taken things up a notch. These guys pose as legit operators to cheat the system on a much bigger scale.

VO: Transporter Anton Eicker never saw it coming. His company provides trucks to move a range of commodities for a number of clients. Coal is part of his core business.

In May, his company was approached by a sub-contractor, Shiyeka Enterprises, offering its trucks to transport coal.

ANTON: We did all the background checks, everything checked out, everything was in order.

VO: Within two weeks the sub-contractor collected 50 loads of coal from a mine destined for a coal terminal at Richards Bay in KZN.

BUT the 50 loads were never delivered – all the paperwork confirming deliveries was forged.

ANTON: At some point, we realized that the receiving stamp at Richardsbay. Was not this same that should have been on the document? So that's when we realized that something was wrong and we requested all the tracking reports from them.

VO: But the tracking data didn’t add up either.

ANTON: All the reports are exactly the same. The loading time. The route down to Richardsbay offloading them back again, loading everything was exactly the same except that registration number was changed on the documents.

VO: In other words, at least 23 trucks were all in the exact same GPS location, at exactly the same time…

LINK: this is no technical error - it’s just a really arrogant attempt to cover their tracks - or rather the tracks they didn’t travel.

Look here - basically - they duplicated one tracking record and changed just the truck’s registration number.

Even the ODO METER readings are identical. Some rookie mistakes for such a sophisticated con…

VO: Take a look at this weighbridge loading slip. The truck’s registration number is KNG127MP. Here it says on the 17 of June 2023 at four minutes past 05 in the afternoon it was loading 34 tons of coal at a mine in Mpumalanga.

Now look at the tracking record for the same truck. On the same date, just six minutes later, this truck was supposedly Richards Bay - more than 500 kilometers away..

The explanation is really simple, but extremely devious.

INSIDER: They was loading the coal, but it didn’t go to Richardsbay.

VO: This is a former employee of the shady sub-contractor. Not a single load of coal ever left Mpumalanga.

INSIDER: They were selling the coal. They were loading at the mine and coming back to the yard
GOVAN So you guys saw trucks with coal at the yard?
INSIDER : Then when they get to the buyer, the trucks they are moving to offload and then they're coming back sometimes to change the number plates and go back to load as other trucks.

VO: So, they were changing the number plates on their trucks to make it look like a bigger non-existing fleet to maximise their thieving efforts.

In this case, it seems this sub-contractor got the job with the sole purpose of stealing.

PAUSE TWO SECONDS

VO: Investigations confirmed that ANton’s company was not the only one targeted using this brazen new MO.

Hans Ebersohn is a transport coordinator for Eicker Transport.

HANS: We find out that this happened to two other companies as well. A subcontractor came in, and then they did the same M.O. and they never went to go offload the loads where it. It was supposed to be offloaded.
GOVAN: That’s almost identical to what happened to you guys.
HANS: Yah - some of the same number plates were used to steal coal from other companies as well

VO: This criminal network made off with over 14000 tones between the other targeted two transporters

GOVAN: How much is that worth?
HANS: In total, it's around about R10.5 million.
GOVAN: Sjoh.

VO: Despite using the same MO, the same sub contractor company wasn’t used.

HANS: There's four different role players in this organization. it's not always the same person. they change around who approaches which company.

VO: Mining Security Consultant Schalk Du Preez isn’t surprised. This is the ultimate evolution of Coal Theft.

SCHALK: The syndicates, all well organized, well-equipped, well-funded and well-armed. They go to an extent to find specialists to bypass any, uh, technical counter security measures that's implemented by either the transporters or the mines. They find experts and they get around it.

VO: Stealing is a standard operating procedure out in Coal Country.

The insider saw it first hand with the Eicker Transport job.

GOVAN: Who’s organising all of this?
INSIDER: The owner of the contract to take the coal is Ntokhozo Buthelezi. So he's working through// the owner of the trucks. They know everything what they are doing.

VO: Ntokhozo Buthelezi is the registered owner of Shiyeka Enterprises - it appears that he was the frontman SPECIFICALLY in the Eicker Transport con… so, we’re going to look for him.

GOVAN: There's a registered business address for Shiyeka here in Witbank.Here we go. This is it. On the left. Oh, no ways… looks like it's this block of flats.

GOVAN: These are always the tell tale signs of dodgy business - registered in a residential area

VO: But we’ve got a second location for the truck yard - it’s in a semi industrial area in Witbank.

GOVAN DRIVING…. It's not even a sign here. Well, the gates open. There's no sign stopping us from entering, so.

GOVAN Alright, this is definitely their operation,
GOVAN The yard is full of old trucks. We just saw a coal truck going out, so….
GOVAN Here comes another one, no - something is happening here // let’s go see…

GUY: I DON’T DO CAMERAS
GOVAN: EINTLIK, Who's the boss around here, bro? We just want to speak to someone who's running this yard.

LINK: They have no OFFICE. It's just a yard with broken trucks.

LINK: These guys obviously know more than they're letting on. They confirm Ntokhozo’s partners still come here. But Ntokhozo’s not here himself. Luckily, we have his number.

GOVAN: Listen Ntokhozo. We know about your dealings with the the transporting company and that they've opened the case against you for stealing 50 loads of coal.
NTOKHOZO: What?
GOVAN: The tracking was fake. You never went to Richards Bay.
NTOKHOZO: I don't have trucks. I'm, I’m a broker.
GOVAN: You can't just say it's the transporters. Chief, you worked with them. You guys stole the coal.
NTOKHOZO: My man, I don't know with them to stealing, I don’t steal coal, I don’t know anything about the coal.

VO: He kept shifting the blame to the truck owners – offering up their contact details.

UPsOUND: Welcome to voice mail… you have reached the mailbox of //The number you have called is not available on the MTN network… GOVAN whistles…..

LINK: //Ntokhozo are sold as a dummy. All these numbers are off.

ANTON: It makes me a little bit furious because these guys just come walk in, steal 1.1 million of coal.// At the end of the day, I'm responsible for the coal because it was in my care.

VO: And that means transporters like Anton also carry the financial loss while the real thieves disappear with the profits gained from their criminality.

LINK: These syndicates operate in silos – it’s middlemen, brokers, drivers and receivers and then off course the money men – the buyers. But they create this web of operators, that makes it near impossible to pin the deal on one kingpin.

VO: That means, right now, this is a crime simply too easy to get away with.

The black Market for it is a lucrative one. SCHALK: if there's no market, then there's no draw, no carrot for the thieves to steal the coal. VO: But criminal syndicates are increasingly inventive with new tactics. We uncover a brand new MO - never exposed before. PROMO 3 VO: Coal theft’s evolved into a sophisticated criminal operation. metadata.Summary: We know the drill - opportunistic criminals target transport company drivers to steal loads and loads of coal for a fee. BUT now, the expose the latest trend. The real coal mafia is hard work as coal theft has evolved into a sophisticated criminal network – the modus operandi have morphed and we will be exposing a brand new one.
metadata.Further information: COAL THEFT 3.0 - THE EVOLUTION OF COAL THEFT UNDERSTANDING THE PROCESS 1. Transporters will be contracted to move tons of coal from a mine (POINT A) to a processing plant or power station or railway station for export (POINT B). 2. Collection slips are issued when the trucks are loaded at POINT A. 3. At POINT B – delivery notes are issued when the loads are dropped off. THE THEFT - not all the loads make it from POINT A to POINT B. Some loads are stolen out right while others switched with a lesser grade of coal. a. Drivers are approached by a middleman to drop the load off at another location along the route between A & B for a fee of R2500 – R12000. b. Delivery notes are jippo-ed and the receiving company at POINT B is none the wiser of the loss. COAL THEFT 3.0 THE EVOLUTION OF COAL THEFT This time round criminal syndicates have streamlined their thieving operations. THE NEW MO 1. A legitimate transporter has a contract from a mine to move coal from Point A to Point B. In this case from Belfast to Richardsbay for export. 2. This transporter is approached by a smaller transport company with 15 trucks asking for work – the transporter does due diligence, and appoints the smaller company as a sub-contractor. 3. The sub-contractor collects 50 loads from the mine, and gives the transporter that contracted them all the paper work stating the load were delivered – the stamped delivery notes, photos of the sealed loads – everything that’s required. BUT ALL IS NOT AS IT SEEMS The mine contacts the transporter – 50 loads were never received – the paper work was forged. No loads collected by the sub-contractor was EVER delivered. Those 50 loads were stolen. THIS SUB-CONTRACTOR GOT THE JOB WITH THE SOLE PURPOSE OF STEALING!!! HOW BIG IS THE PROBLEM? This is not an isolated problem – coal theft plagues the industry across South Africa. The black market for coal is thriving because there is a huge demand for coal locally and for export. So if you can get a cheap load that you can sell at premium prices – dodgy dealers are willing to look the other way. LOSSES The stolen loads would have been paid for the company meant to receive the cargo because the paperwork in terms of the jippo-ed delivery notes will check out. But the dodgy dealers buying the stolen loads will then re-sell the cargo back into the market – essentially one loads would be paid for TWICE! Because there are insiders involved, the paperwork checks out – but it is only when stock takes are done by the receiving companies that the losses are noted. For example, a company would have paid for 100 000 tones, but only received 80 000. INTERVIEWS INDUSTRY EXPERT – SCHALK DU PREEZ DU PREEZ heads up the coal theft investigations for a group of mines - he will explain the black market and how these syndicates have evolved their modus operandi’s incorporating tech and elaborate schemes to steal coal – it’s no longer the odd dodgy driver – it’s the coal mafia at work. TRANSPORTER – ANTON EICKER WE GO IN SEARCH OF SHIYEKA ENTERPRISES ** ADDITIONAL SHOOT INTERVIEW WITH TRACKER Confirming the tracking logs were forged. INTERVIEW OPS MANAGER OF THE TRANSPORTER They’ve been able to find at three more transporters were the same MO was used – not necessarily the same broker, but the same method – getting a contract with the sole purpose of stealing, using fake number plates – some of which correspond with Eicker Transport. ** ADDITONAL LINKS ** ADDITIONAL B-ROLL EXTRA COSTS DAY TRIP TO MPUMALANGA
